passage: Playground note by Farida, nursery helper. At the games corner, Nandini lost the ring-toss to a classmate. She dropped the last ring, turned her back and walked to the far fence, arms stiff. I noticed she kept looking at the game from a distance. I didn't follow. After a few minutes I called, "Nandini, we'd like you back for the next round if you want." She waited, then came back and stood at the edge before rejoining. I think she was upset and needed a little time, though she may also have been embarrassed.

qa.q: What game did Nandini lose?
qa.a: She lost the ring-toss to a classmate.

qa.q: What might Nandini have been feeling when she turned her back and walked to the far fence?
qa.a: She was probably upset or embarrassed about losing, and needed space. She kept looking back at the game, which suggests she still wanted to be part of it.

qa.q: What did Farida do that gave Nandini space without pushing her away?
qa.a: Farida didn't follow, then invited Nandini back with a calm call and left the choice to Nandini.

qa.q: How might the classmate who won see Nandini walking off?
qa.a: They may feel confused or a bit guilty, unless an adult explains that Nandini just needs a moment.

grounding: A child walks off after a lost game, and a calm invitation to return works better than following with demands.

passage: In the hill village of Mizoram, Lalremsiami, five, was told off for taking her cousin's slate and she turned to the wall. Then she walked out, past the shoes at the door, and sat on the step by the chickens. Her grandmother Damini stayed inside stirring the pot, and watched through the doorway. After a few minutes she called softly, "The rice is ready when you are." Lalremsiami stayed a bit longer, then wandered in, and leaned on Damini's knee without a word.

qa.q: Where did Lalremsiami sit after walking out?
qa.a: She sat on the step by the chickens.

qa.q: What might Lalremsiami have been feeling when she turned to the wall and walked out?
qa.a: She may have felt embarrassed or upset about being told off and wanted space. She might also have felt cross that she was told off.

qa.q: Why did Damini stay in the kitchen and call softly?
qa.a: She gave Lalremsiami room to calm down and a way back without demanding an apology, and Lalremsiami came in on her own.

qa.q: How might the cousin see Lalremsiami walking away?
qa.a: The cousin may think she is angry or feel a little guilty, and would understand better if someone explained she wanted space.

grounding: A young child walks off after a rebuke, and a calm invitation to return works better than following with demands.

passage: At the park in Seoul, Jin and Zeynep raced to the slide. Zeynep touched it first. Jin stopped, turned his back and walked off to the bench, shoulders stiff. His father didn't follow him with questions. He waited a minute, then called in a calm voice, “Jin, the slide's still here when you're ready. Zeynep's waiting for a rematch.” Jin sat for a while, kicking the sand. Then he got up, walked slowly back and said, “Best of three.”

qa.q: Where did Jin walk off to?
qa.a: To the bench.

qa.q: What might Jin have been feeling as he walked off with stiff shoulders?
qa.a: He was probably disappointed and embarrassed about losing the race, and wanted some space. He might also have felt a bit angry at himself.

qa.q: Why did the father's calm invitation work?
qa.a: He gave Jin space and time instead of following him with demands, and left the door open to come back.

qa.q: How might Zeynep have felt when Jin walked away?
qa.a: She might have felt confused or worried that he was angry with her, and relieved when he came back for a rematch.

grounding: A young child turns away and walks off after losing a race, and a calm invitation to return works.

passage: Sports hour at the community centre: Ujjwal grabbed the big red ball. “That one's for the older group,” said Rajni, the coach. Ujjwal dropped it, turned round and walked to the far corner, his face to the wall. Rajni didn't go after him. She set up the small balls and called out, “Ujjwal, when you're ready, there's a green ball with your name on it.” Ujjwal stayed in the corner, then peeped over his shoulder. A few minutes later he came back and picked up the green ball.

qa.q: What colour ball did Rajni offer Ujjwal?
qa.a: A green ball.

qa.q: What does Ujjwal walking off to face the wall suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt upset and embarrassed after being refused the big ball, and needed a moment alone. It could also have been anger at the rule.

qa.q: What could Rajni do next time to avoid the upset?
qa.a: She could explain before the game which balls are for which group, so the refusal doesn't come as a surprise.

qa.q: What would change if Rajni had followed him and insisted he play?
qa.a: Ujjwal might dig in and refuse, and the upset would last longer.

grounding: A young child walks off after a refusal, and his coach's calm invitation to return works better than following him.

passage: I'm Swati, Neelam's cousin. At the fair, Neelam's mother said no to a second ice cream. Neelam turned her back and walked away toward the gate, arms swinging hard. I thought she'd get lost, but her mother just kept her in sight and called, “Neelam, I'm here by the swings when you're ready.” Neelam stood at the gate for a minute, then came back and leaned against her mother's side. I couldn't tell if she was angry or sad, but she held her mother's hand after that.

qa.q: What did Neelam's mother say no to?
qa.a: A second ice cream.

qa.q: What might Neelam have been feeling when she walked away toward the gate?
qa.a: She might have been angry or sad, or both, and wanted space after the refusal. Swati could not tell which.

qa.q: Which choice by Neelam's mother worked?
qa.a: She kept Neelam in sight and gave a calm invitation to return instead of chasing her with demands.

qa.q: How might Swati have felt watching Neelam walk off?
qa.a: Swati felt worried that Neelam might get lost, and was relieved when she came back.

grounding: A cousin observes a young child walk off after a refusal, and her mother's calm invitation brings her back.

passage:
Monday: Samir lost at carrom and walked straight out of the room. Bhupen Chacha followed him down the corridor. "Come back! Say good game! Don't be a bad loser!" Samir ran into the bedroom and slammed the door.

Thursday: Samir lost again and turned away. This time Chacha stayed put. "The board's here when you're ready." A few minutes later, Samir crept back and sat down.

The next Sunday: Samir lost, frowned hard at the board, and stayed. "Again," he said.

qa.q: What game did Samir lose?
qa.a: Carrom.

qa.q: What was Samir probably feeling when he walked out after losing?
qa.a: He was most likely upset and embarrassed about losing. On Monday, being followed with demands seemed to make him feel more cornered, so he slammed the door.

qa.q: What went wrong on Monday, and what fixed it later?
qa.a: Following Samir with demands pushed him further away; a calm invitation on Thursday gave him space and he came back on his own.

qa.q: How does Bhupen Chacha's approach change between Monday and Thursday?
qa.a: On Monday he chases Samir and lectures him, but on Thursday he stays put and leaves the door open for him to return.

grounding: It shows a young child walking off after losing and a calm invitation to come back working better than following with demands.
